paragraphs.source_en: Concerning the scarcity of the pottery, the Barich (1998b) and Close's (1995) statement of the symbolical use is one possible explanation. However, it is also possible that pottery in the Early Holocene was much more abundant but consisted mainly of unfired pots that did not survive until today. As Rice (1999) points out, the earliest recovered evidence of clay manipulation in the world consists of unfired or low-fired objects such as figurines, some dating to as early as 28,000 BP in Europe1. Low-fired or unfired clay utensils may have been more widespread in prehistoric times but they would not have left traces in the archaeological record. These pots might have been sufficiently durable to be used for several years, and replaced by new ones when they broke.

paragraphs.source_en: In the Central Sahara unfired ceramics may have been produced and used before the fired pottery appeared in the 10th millennium BP, and the two technologies may have coexisted. The invention of high fired pottery might have been more easily made if unfired clay objects were already known. If so, why were certain containers fired to make them durable? The answer may lie in the importance given to various vessels and their use. The more important containers used for important occasions were more likely to be high-fired, and this presumed importance would be confirmed by the fact that virtually all of the earliest pottery in the Central Sahara is decorated. The existence, in prehistoric times, of unfired containers together with high-fired ones may explain the scarcity of the earliest pottery found today.

paragraphs.source_en: Scholars generally consider the excellent quality of the Saharan pottery as a final stage of a tradition, the origins of which must be searched for elsewhere. However, these presumed origins have not yet been found outside the Central Sahara which may be due to a lack of excavation, but it may also suggest that pottery earlier than the 10th-11th millennium BP simply does not exist. The earliest pottery dating to the 10th millennium BP may indicate not the invention of the tradition but the starting point from which some of the previously unfired vessels were high-fired, i. e. a change in the production technique. It may explain the seemingly sudden appearance of the pottery in the Central Sahara.
